descriptions.value: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. Through 9.0.4, ZipArchive treats Central Directory File Header filenames as authoritative while ZipStreamReader extracts using Local File Header filenames without reconciling the duplicate metadata in src/read/stream.rs. A crafted archive can therefore appear benign to a component that inspects the central directory but cause a streaming extractor to write a different attacker-selected path and content, potentially overwriting files used by a downstream service. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.5.

cna.title: Low privilege condition filter escapes Twig sandbox, recovers "securityKey" and reaches RCE

descriptions.value:
Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose element selector is evaluated as a sandboxed Twig object template. Craft’s allowed column filter delegates property lookup to Yii ArrayHelper, outside Twig’s SecurityPolicy. Repeated single-segment lookups therefore bypass the sandbox’s empty property/method allowlists.



The vulnerable condition value is ultimately cast to an integer. That does not protect the secret: the template can return author ID 1 when a guessed key character is correct and an impossible ID otherwise. The JSON endpoint returns entries for the first case and an empty array for the second, forming a stable remote character oracle.



After recovering GeneralConfig::securityKey, the same user can compute Craft’s generic HMAC wire format offline. Signed parameters such as redirect are then accepted and passed to unsandboxed View::renderObjectTemplate(), where Twig’s string-callable form can invoke native PHP callables. The regression proof uses the harmless substr() callback and observes abcdef becoming cdef; it does not execute an OS command.

descriptions.value: P-Net before 1.0.3 does not check that a complete block header is present in the received data before reading the next block in DCP Set and Identify requests. cna.title: Apache ZooKeeper: Unbounded recursion in snapshot serialization allows a client to render the server unrecoverable

credits.value: Sai Sreewathsa Kovalluri, Shon Babu, and Kannan K of Innspark Solutions (https://innspark.in/)
Prasath Jayasundar & PayPal Cyber Security Team

descriptions.value:
Uncontrolled recursion in Apache ZooKeeper. The server serializes its data tree to a snapshot by recursing one stack frame per znode level, with no depth bound. A client permitted to create znodes (the default root ACL is open) can build a chain of nested znodes deep enough that taking a snapshot exhausts the JVM stack and kills the snapshot thread; sizes stay within jute.maxbuffer, so existing limits do not prevent it. This is a denial of service that becomes persistent: on restart the server rebuilds the deep tree from its transaction log and fails again while taking the startup snapshot, so it does not return to service, and recovery can entail data loss. The same log affects a leader and its followers, so it can spread across an ensemble.

This issue affects Apache ZooKeeper 3.8.0 through 3.8.7 and 3.9.0 through 3.9.6. Users are recommended to upgrade to 3.8.8 or 3.9.7, which fix the issue. As a workaround, use ACLs and authentication to restrict znode creation rather than relying on the default open root ACL.

cna.title: Pocket ID: Email verification token remains valid after address change, enabling arbitrary verified-email spoofing

descriptions.description: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

descriptions.value: Pocket ID is an OIDC provider that allows users to authenticate with their passkeys to services. From 2.2.0 until 2.12.0, SendEmailVerification uses the token model in backend/internal/model/email_verification_token.go to bind an email-verification token only to the user's identifier, while UpdateUser can change the account email without invalidating the outstanding token and VerifyEmail marks the current address as verified. An ordinary user can request a token for an address they control, change the account to an arbitrary unused address, and redeem the old token so Pocket ID publishes the new address with email_verified set to true. The default affected configuration uses emailsVerified=false and allowOwnAccountEdit=true; the target address must not already belong to another Pocket ID user. A relying application that trusts a verified email for automatic account matching or provisioning can link the attacker's identity to another user's account, while applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC sub claim are not affected by that downstream consequence. This issue is fixed in version 2.12.0.

descriptions.value:
An unauthenticated SQL injection can occur on the front end of any site that uses craft.search to perform a search, allowing stacked query execution and enabling escalation to an administrator.



Note that this only affects MySQL/MariaDB.

Impact  *  SQL injection — The attribute parameter is concatenated into the query unsanitized, and because PDO runs with emulated prepares, stacked statements execute. This gives unauthenticated read and write access to the application database.
  *  Privilege escalation to administrator — The write primitive was used to set the admin flag on user ID 1 in the users table, confirmed by reading the value back. Craft short-circuits its permission checks on this single column, so no further changes were needed. The same primitive can overwrite any account’s password hash.




Update to the patched versions (4.18.9 and 5.11.2) to get the fix.



If you cannot update immediately, you can block front-end requests with %5Battribute%5D and [attribute] anywhere in the query string as a temporary mitigation.

cna.title: Unverified key-pair binding lets an unauthenticated token user substitute the public key or certificate returned for a private key

descriptions.description: CWE-345 Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

descriptions.value:
In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `<= 2.0.0-rc8` (and the deprecated v1 module paths `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11 <= 1.6.8`, `github.com/ThalesGroup/crypto11 <= 1.7.0-rc1` and `github.com/ThalesIgnite/crypto11 <= 1.2.5`), the key-pair and certificate lookup functions (`FindKeyPair`, `FindKeyPairs`, `FindKeyPairsWithAttributes`, `FindAllKeyPairs`, the `FindRSAKeyPair*` family and `FindAllPairedCertificates`) pair a private key with a public key object, or with a certificate, by `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` alone, take the first match the token returns, and never verify that it belongs to the private key. PKCS#11 permits a session that has not logged in to create public token objects, so anyone able to open a session on the token — without the PIN — can plant a public key or certificate carrying a victim key's `CKA_ID` and label, and crypto11 may return it as that key's public half. An application that publishes or trusts `Signer.Public()` (a JWKS endpoint, a key registry, `authorized_keys`, a CSR) then publishes the attacker's key, and relying parties accept anything the attacker signs as coming from the service. On the v1 line the lookup also falls back to a class-and-key-type-only search when the private key has no `CKA_ID`, pairing a label-only private key with the first public key of its type on the token.



The v1 module paths are deprecated and will not be fixed; users should migrate to github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2 version 2.0.0-rc9 or later.

cna.title: Twisted: HTTP Request Smuggling in twisted.web via a Bare CR or LF in a Header Value

descriptions.description: CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

descriptions.value: Twisted is an event-based framework for internet applications, supporting Python 3.6+. Prior to 26.10.0rc1, twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel.headerReceived rejects a NUL byte in an HTTP header value but accepts a bare carriage return or bare line feed. Because Twisted splits header lines only on CRLF, a hidden Content-Length header can remain folded into another value while a lenient front end treats the bare character as a line terminator. The resulting framing disagreement can smuggle a following request past front-end access controls, poison a shared connection or cache, and expose a later client to the wrong response. This issue is an incomplete-fix residual of earlier Twisted request-smuggling protections. This issue is fixed in version 26.10.0rc1.

cna.title: Cluster-API proxy overwrites forwarded client identity with its own

solutions.value: Upgrade applications using github.com/moby/swarmkit/v2 to version 2.1.3 or later.

descriptions.value: SwarmKit's Cluster-API proxy can overwrite a forwarded client's TLS identity with an intermediary manager's identity. WithMetadataForwardTLSInfo replaces outgoing metadata with a copy of the incoming metadata, discarding the redirect guard's changes when built with grpc-go 1.39 or later. During a short window after a leader change, two proxy hops through managers with inconsistent views of the leader can allow an attacker possessing a valid worker node TLS certificate and private key to obtain a manager node certificate for the attacker's own key, escalating privileges from worker to manager. cna.title: zip: AES Entry HMAC Authentication Bypass on Premature EOF

descriptions.value: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 0.6.0 until 9.0.0, the AES entry reader in src/aes.rs verifies its HMAC only when the attacker-controlled data counter reaches zero. If the underlying bounded reader reaches the real end of the archive while data_remaining is still positive, or if an encrypted entry has no payload, the reader can return a clean end of stream without reading and comparing the authentication tag. Applications using by_index_decrypt, by_name_decrypt, by_path_decrypt, or password-enabled by_index_with_options can therefore accept modified plaintext without an authentication error. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

cna.title: Unauthenticated payment reuse allows unpaid orders to be marked as paid

descriptions.value:
The Mollie webhook endpoint accepts two independent, attacker-controlled parameters and never verifies that they belong together:

  *  commerceTransactionHash — selects which Craft Commerce transaction is completed
  *  id — selects which Mollie payment is queried for its status




An unauthenticated attacker holding any paid Mollie payment ID from the merchant’s account can pair it with any transaction hash.



Commerce queries Mollie, sees status: paid, and marks the target transaction successful for that transaction’s full
amount, regardless of how much was actually paid.

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. descriptions.value: Poweradmin is a web-based DNS administration tool for PowerDNS server. cna.title: obsidian-tc: Declined human-in-the-loop confirmations can permit destructive calls over HTTP

descriptions.value: obsidian-tc is a governed, agent-ready Model Context Protocol server for Obsidian vaults. From 1.13.0 until 1.31.4, on a Streamable HTTP deployment with `auth.jwtSecret` configured and a 2026-07-28-era client declaring `elicitation.form` support, a dispatch-gated tool call offered an `inputRequired` confirmation could still complete after the human declined or cancelled, or the elicitation response was omitted or malformed, provided the client echoed the validly bound `requestState` on resubmission. The server trusted an authentic, call-bound state as proof of approval even though that state was minted before the `elicitation/create` leg was asked and proved only that the resubmission belonged to the same call. A client behaving incorrectly or under an attacker's control could therefore execute dispatch-gated destructive vault operations without the human's approval, while still requiring the caller's ordinary tool permissions. Only tools marked `destructive: true` or requiring a scope with a human-in-the-loop floor were reachable through this bypass. The sixteen handler-side conditionally gated tools, including `write_note` overwrite and `move_note`, did not read elicitation state on the modern wire and let neither approval nor decline through that path. Affected deployments using stdio or leaving `auth.jwtSecret` unset instead used the CLI `elicit_token` fallback and did not offer this `requestState` round trip. The fix does not prevent a malicious client from reporting a fabricated approval, because the server cannot verify that the client displayed the form or that a human saw it. This issue is fixed in version 1.31.4.

cna.title: Forged signed tokens let any registered user take over other users and organizations

descriptions.value: A registered user can obtain a validly signed token with claims of their choosing and use it as a login session for another user, without knowing any identifier of the victim when database filter objects are used as claims.

An attacker can join any other organization as super administrator, using an organization id that is exposed by any shared post preview link, read its API key and channel list and schedule posts through its connected social accounts.
An attacker can reset the password of a user whose id they know, and can obtain an organization with a lifetime top-tier subscription through the enterprise provisioning endpoint.
Forged tokens do not expire and cannot be told apart from genuine ones.
The narrower invitation route lets a user who may invite team members repeatedly stop the scheduled posts of a channel of another organization, and lift the channel limit of their own plan.

exploits.value: Exploitation was demonstrated end to end against an unmodified backend build at commit 3a7d28b7ad96: a second self-registered user became super administrator of another user's organization and read its API key. Session, password reset, enterprise and subscription tokens obtained the same way were each accepted by their endpoints.

timeline.value: Anthropic has disclosed a thorough report of this vulnerability including a working PoC to Postiz
Postiz has reproduced the vulnerability and is working on a fix
Postiz has pushed a fix for this vulnerability and verified it
Postiz has created a release and published the advisory

workarounds.value: If you do not use channels that rely on the Postiz browser extension, block POST /integrations/extension-refresh at your reverse proxy. This removes the main signing route; the team invitation route remains.
Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true. The attacker needs an ordinary account, so closing self-registration limits exposure to people who already hold one. This reduces reach, it does not close the issue.

descriptions.value:
Postiz signs its session, invitation and password reset tokens with one shared secret and without any marker of what a token is for. A route that refreshes the credentials of a browser-extension channel signed data taken from the request itself and stored the result where the requesting user can read it back. A user could therefore obtain a validly signed token containing any claims they choose, which the application accepts as a session, as an organization invitation with a chosen role, as a password reset or as an enterprise provisioning token.

A second, narrower route that creates team invitations signs extra fields from the request body in the same way.

configurations.value: The instance must be able to reach api2.skool.com, as any instance using the Skool provider can. No setting has to be changed.

With Stripe billing configured, the attacker's own plan must allow one channel and the target organization must not be on the STANDARD tier. The session and password reset tokens are not affected by these limits.
Self-registration is open unless DISABLE_REGISTRATION is set to true.

cna.title: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Externally-Accessible File or Directory in Elastic Cloud Enterprise (ECE) Leading to Credential Disclosure

descriptions.value: CAPEC-37 Retrieve Embedded Sensitive Data

Insertion of Sensitive Information into Externally-Accessible File or Directory (CWE-538) in Elastic Cloud Enterprise (ECE) can lead to credential disclosure via Retrieve Embedded Sensitive Data (CAPEC-37). ECE stores runtime information about platform service containers in a location that lower-privileged platform components can read, and this information includes secrets from the container configuration. An attacker with access to the internal ECE platform services can obtain these secrets, which include role tokens. A role token can let the attacker add an unauthorized host to the installation with the roles of that token.

cna.title: Apache Kafka: Connect Admin REST API Authentication Bypass via Unapplied REST Extensions

descriptions.value:
Apache Kafka Connect contains an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the admin REST API when admin.listeners is configured with a separate listener from the main listeners property.

When operators isolate the admin REST API by explicitly configuring the "admin.listeners" property, REST extensions specified via rest.extension.classes (such as BasicAuthSecurityRestExtension) are not registered or applied to the admin resource configuration.

While the primary REST API listener (configured via listeners) enforces configured authentication and authorization filters, endpoints mounted under the separate admin listener (/admin/loggers) fail to inherit or instantiate these extension filters. As a result, the admin logger endpoint accepts unauthenticated read and write requests even when security extensions are active on the main listener.

Impact:

An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the admin listener can:

  1. Read the complete set of logger names and levels, disclosing loaded class names and which security extensions are in use.
  2. Write logger levels, including with scope=cluster which propagates the change to all workers in the Connect cluster. This can be used to suppress
     logging (setting root to OFF) or generate excessive log output (setting root to TRACE), potentially impacting availability and observability.

Mitigation:

  Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove the admin.listeners configuration (or leave it unset). When unset, admin resources share the regular listener and inherit its security extensions.

Resolution:


From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, and 4.4.0, we make sure the REST extensions specified via "rest.extension.classes" will also apply to "admin.listeners".

cna.title: Cowboy HTTP/1.1 Unbounded Buffering of Pipelined Data During Request Handling Enables Memory Exhaustion

descriptions.value: An unauthenticated remote client can make one connection process hold an arbitrary amount of memory by sending data after a request while its handler runs. A few such connections to an endpoint that holds requests open exhaust node memory and terminate every connection served by that node.

descriptions.value:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ninenines cowboy allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust connection process memory over HTTP/1.1.

Once a request has been received in full and its handler is still running, cowboy_http:parse/2 in src/cowboy_http.erl appends every further byte that arrives on the keep-alive connection to the connection buffer and returns to the receive loop without parsing it. The socket stays in active mode and no limit applies to this buffer: max_request_line_length, max_headers and the other parser limits only take effect once the handler returns and parsing resumes, and the only timer in this state is idle_timeout (default 60 seconds), which is reset on every received chunk. A client can therefore send an arbitrary amount of data on one connection for as long as the handler runs, and a few connections to an endpoint that holds requests open can drive the Erlang VM into out-of-memory conditions.

This issue affects cowboy: from 2.18.0 before 2.21.0.

configurations.value: The amount of data buffered scales with how long the current handler keeps the connection busy. Any HTTP/1.1 endpoint exposes a window, but deployments with handlers that hold a request open, such as long polling with cowboy_loop, streamed responses via cowboy_req:stream_reply/3, or slow backend calls, give an attacker the time to buffer significant memory. HTTP/2 connections are not affected.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Start a cowboy HTTP/1.1 listener with a handler that takes time to reply, for example one that sleeps 20 seconds before calling cowboy_req:reply/4.
* Open one TCP connection and send a complete GET / HTTP/1.1 request with a Host header.
* While the handler is still running, keep writing arbitrary bytes on the same connection, for example 300 one-megabyte chunks.
* Inspect the connection process with erlang:process_info/2 while the handler runs: its referenced binaries grow by the amount sent and erlang:memory(binary) rises by the same amount. No parser limit or timeout interrupts the transfer.
* When the handler replies, the client still receives the 200 OK; only afterwards does the buffered data get parsed and rejected.

On 2.16.1 and 2.17.0 step 3 is cut short: the server answers 414 Request-URI Too Long with connection: close as soon as the first chunk arrives and holds nothing.

2. Open one TCP connection and send a complete `GET / HTTP/1.1` request with a `Host` header.

4. Inspect the connection process with `erlang:process_info/2` while the handler runs: its referenced binaries grow by the amount sent and `erlang:memory(binary)` rises by the same amount. No parser limit or timeout interrupts the transfer.
5. When the handler replies, the client still receives the `200 OK`; only afterwards does the buffered data get parsed and rejected.

On 2.16.1 and 2.17.0 step 3 is cut short: the server answers `414 Request-URI Too Long` with `connection: close` as soon as the first chunk arrives and holds nothing.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Request completes, handler runs. When cowboy_http finishes reading a request it moves the parser to the ps_next_request state while the stream for that request is still alive. The connection process keeps the socket in active mode (setopts_active/1 re-arms {active, N} whenever a passive notification arrives), so the VM continues to deliver socket data to the process.

2. Data is appended, never parsed. Each incoming chunk reaches loop/1, which concatenates it onto the connection buffer and calls parse/2. The parse/2 clause for in_state=ps_next_request with a live #stream{} returns straight to before_loop/1 with the enlarged buffer, deferring all parsing until the current stream stops. The parser limits (max_request_line_length, max_header_name_length, max_header_value_length, max_headers) are enforced only by the parsing clauses that run after that point, and max_skip_body_length only covers an unread body of the current request, not bytes after it.

3. No timer bounds the window. While a stream is live the connection runs on idle_timeout (default 60 seconds), and set_timeout/2 resets it on every received chunk. The attacker therefore keeps the window open by continuing to send. Only the handler finishing ends it, at which point parsing resumes, the buffered bytes fail the request-line checks, and the connection closes with a 4xx response. By then the data has been held for the full handler duration.

4. Introduction. The behaviour arrived with the change that removed concurrent processing of pipelined HTTP/1.1 requests (first shipped in 2.18.0). Earlier releases parsed pipelined data as it arrived, so excess bytes hit the request-line limit immediately and the connection was closed with 414 Request-URI Too Long before any significant amount was buffered. The introducing commit describes the intended behaviour as stopping reads from the socket until the stream stops, but the code keeps the socket active and buffers instead.

cna.title: Open-iscsi: open-iscsi: ipv6 neighbor discovery missing option length validation in iscsiuio allows arp table poisoning

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Tristan Madani (Talence Security) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Keep iscsiuio-managed interfaces on trusted L2 segments only. Where operationally acceptable, filter ICMPv6 Neighbor Advertisement (type 136) and Neighbor Solicitation (type 135) messages from untrusted sources using firewall rules.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the iscsiuio component of open-iscsi. The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery handler accesses link-layer address options at a fixed offset without verifying the packet contains them. Additionally, the ARP table is updated unconditionally with attacker-controlled addresses from the packet headers. An attacker on the same network segment can send a minimal Neighbor Advertisement to poison the ARP table and redirect network traffic.

cna.title: Wasmtime: Cranelift backend on aarch64 can jump to incorrect target on large Wasm `br_table` instruction

descriptions.value: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. Prior to 36.0.19, 48.0.7, and 49.0.4, the Cranelift compiler backend on aarch64 can compile a Wasm br_table instruction with more than approximately 256,000 targets so that it has an incorrect conditional branch target. The branch can then jump to arbitrary other code at a user-controlled offset, allowing a user-controlled Wasm module to escape the sandbox on aarch64 engines using the default Cranelift backend. This issue is fixed in versions 36.0.19, 48.0.7, and 49.0.4.

cna.title: ML-KEM key-pair lookup can bind an unrelated or attacker-planted public key, exposing encapsulated shared secrets

descriptions.value: In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `>= 2.0.0-rc3, <= 2.0.0-rc8`, the ML-KEM key-pair lookup functions (`FindMLKEMKeyPair`, `FindMLKEMKeyPairs`, `FindMLKEMKeyPairsWithAttributes`) locate the public half of an ML-KEM key pair by `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` and never verify it against the private key. In addition, the "ID only" fallback search runs even when the private key has no `CKA_ID`, so the search template reduces to the public-key class and the ML-KEM key type and the first ML-KEM public key on the token is returned. `Encapsulate()` on the resulting key pair encrypts the fresh shared secret to that key, so its owner — not the holder of the private key the caller looked up — can recover the secret. An attacker who can open an unauthenticated session on the token and plant a public `CKK_ML_KEM` object carrying the victim's `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` receives the shared secrets for encapsulations performed through the substituted key pair, compromising the confidentiality of those secrets and of everything protected by keys derived from them. The v1 module paths have no ML-KEM support and are not affected.

cna.title: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information in Elasticsearch Leading to Information Disclosure

descriptions.value: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information (CWE-524) in Elasticsearch can lead to information disclosure and incorrect search results via specially crafted search requests. For some query types, Elasticsearch can share cached query results between users who have field-level security restrictions and users who do not. A user restricted by field-level security can learn which documents match a value in a field that they cannot read. A restricted user can also cause users with full access to receive incomplete search results. Disclosure is only possible when a user with full access ran the same query on the same shard recently.

cna.title: Contact Form by Supsystic < 1.11.1 - Admin+ SSTI via Form Text Block

descriptions.value: The Contact Form by Supsystic  WordPress plugin before 1.11.1 does not sandbox the template engine used to render its forms and allows stored form-editor content to reach that engine as executable template code, enabling an administrator to perform server-side template injection and execute arbitrary code on the server. The injected template is compiled and executed whenever any visitor loads a page containing the form, so the stored payload also lets an unauthenticated visitor read server-side secrets such as authentication salts and database credentials.

cna.title: Spreadsheet::XLSX versions before 0.19 for Perl allow code execution via string eval of number format conditions in ExcelFmt

solutions.value: Upgrade to Spreadsheet-XLSX 0.19 or later.

descriptions.value:
Spreadsheet::XLSX versions before 0.19 for Perl allow code execution via string eval of number format conditions in ExcelFmt.

When a number format has a condition such as [>100], ExcelFmt chooses the format section by passing the condition and the cell value to a string eval. Both come from the workbook, and the eval runs while Spreadsheet::XLSX->new parses it.

An attacker who supplies an XLSX file can run arbitrary Perl code.

workarounds.value: There are no official workarounds. To reduce the risk without upgrading, restrict administrative access (including permissions to manage segments and custom fields, and API access) to trusted users, and make sure no untrusted party has write access to the Mautic database.

supportingMedia.value: There are no official workarounds. To reduce the risk without upgrading, restrict administrative access (including permissions to manage segments and custom fields, and API access) to trusted users, and make sure no untrusted party has write access to the Mautic database.

descriptions.value: An insecure deserialization (PHP object injection) vulnerability exists in Mautic's handling of segment filters and custom field properties. Several code paths that read these stored values from the database deserialize them without restricting which PHP classes may be instantiated, instead of using Mautic's safe deserialization helper. An attacker who is able to store a crafted serialized value in these segment filter or custom field properties can cause arbitrary PHP objects to be instantiated when Mautic later processes the data, for example during segment evaluation, contact export, or custom field API requests. Combined with gadget chains available in Mautic's dependencies, this could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server, read, modify, or delete data stored in the Mautic instance, including contact data, and affect its availability. Exploitation requires high privileges or an existing ability to write to the affected stored data.

descriptions.value: @hapi/content from 6.0.1 before 6.0.3 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in Content.disposition() caused by an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-35213. Unauthenticated remote attackers can send multipart uploads with a long Content-Disposition parameter lacking an equals sign, triggering quadratic backtracking that blocks the event loop.

cna.title: XS::libbrotli versions before 1.2.1.0 for Perl bundle a brotli library with an out-of-bounds write in the decoder

solutions.value: Upgrade to XS-libbrotli 1.2.1.0 or later and reinstall every XS module built against it.

descriptions.value:
XS::libbrotli versions before 1.2.1.0 for Perl bundle a brotli library with an out-of-bounds write in the decoder.

Affected versions compile a bundled brotli into static archives that dependent XS modules link against at build time, rather than using the system library. The bundled copy, 1.0.7 or 1.1.0 across the range, carries the decoder out-of-bounds write described in CVE-2026-111497. Version 1.2.1.0 updates it to brotli 1.2.1.

XS::libbrotli has no Perl interface, so the decoder is reached through any dependent module that decompresses untrusted data with it. An attacker supplying a crafted brotli stream can corrupt decoder state, disclose memory, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. Upgrading the system brotli does not remediate this.

descriptions.value: Frappe Builder before 1.36.1 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in builder/api.py where the assert_not_private_url() guard validates only the initial hostname before callers invoke requests.get(url) with default redirect-following and no IP pinning, allowing an attacker-supplied public URL to HTTP-redirect to internal or link-local addresses the guard never validated. An authenticated attacker can call the convert_to_webp endpoint, which lacks a permission decorator, with a URL that redirects to internal targets such as cloud metadata services to perform SSRF, internal port scanning, or trigger a request-hang denial of service due to the missing timeout.

affected.product: User Profile Builder – Beautiful User Registration Forms, User Profiles & User Role Editor

descriptions.value: The User Profile Builder – Beautiful User Registration Forms, User Profiles & User Role Editor plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Limited Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 4.0.3. This is due to the Gutenberg Register block passing the attacker-controlled Assigned Role attribute directly into the `[wppb-register]` shortcode without server-side authorization. The role guard in the form builder only downgrades roles that carry the manage_options or remove_users capability, leaving the Editor role and other privileged non-Administrator roles completely unrestricted. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers with Author-level access and above to create new WordPress accounts bearing the Editor role (or any other role that lacks the two guarded capabilities).

descriptions.value: ConnMan through 2.0 has a stack-based buffer overflow via a DHCPv6 Reply message. This occurs in get_domains in gdhcp/client.c. It copies a fixed NS_MAXDNAME (1025) bytes from a DHCPv6 DOMAIN_LIST (option 24) value into a 1026-byte stack buffer dns_name regardless of the actual option length, then walks DNS labels with an unbounded "c += jump + 1" loop. A crafted DHCPv6 REPLY with a DOMAIN_LIST option of >= 1025 non-zero bytes makes the label walk leave the buffer and read/write '.' past its end in attacker-chosen strides. An on-link attacker can trigger this without authentication via a forged Router Advertisement (O=1) and a forged DHCPv6 REPLY matching xid/CLIENTID with a long DOMAIN_LIST. The impact is unauthenticated on-link crash of connmand (runs as root). This was introduced in bb06c47.

cna.title: zip: Unbounded Symlink-Target Handling Can Abort Or Exhaust Memory During Extraction

descriptions.value: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 1.3.0 until 9.0.0, ZipArchive::extract in src/read/mod.rs calls Vec::with_capacity for a symbolic link target using the attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed_size before reading entry data. A small archive can request an impossible capacity, causing the infallible allocation path to abort the process before the entry is validated. The failure cannot be contained with catch_unwind or a worker thread, allowing repeated denial of service in archive-processing applications. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

cna.title: Twisted: Denial of Service in the Twisted IMAP4 Server via a Negative Literal Size in SEARCH

descriptions.value: Twisted is an event-based framework for internet applications, supporting Python 3.6+. Prior to 26.10.0rc1, twisted.mail.imap4.IMAP4Server reaches twisted.mail.imap4.parseNestedParens with a negative literal size in an authenticated SEARCH command after the client enters the selected mailbox state. The negative size moves the parser cursor below zero, and Python's negative indexing prevents the synchronous scanning loop from terminating. The loop freezes the single-threaded reactor, stopping other IMAP connections and any SMTP or POP3 services hosted in the same process until restart. This issue is fixed in version 26.10.0rc1.

cna.title: draw.io: Prototype pollution in GraphML (mxGraphMlCodec)

descriptions.value: draw.io is a configurable diagramming and whiteboarding application. Prior to 31.1.5, the GraphML decoder contains a prototype-pollution vulnerability. Attacker-controlled GraphML reference keys can address inherited object properties, including prototype objects, and the decoder can then assign attacker-controlled attributes to those objects. Importing a malicious GraphML file can trigger client-side prototype pollution. In the advisory-supported cross-site scripting chain, the editor is opened in Trello mode and the user invokes the Trello integration after the import, allowing the polluted state to execute script in the draw.io origin; an existing Trello connection is not required. This vulnerability is fixed in 31.1.5.

cna.title: zip: Arbitrary file write outside the extraction directory, because ZipArchive::extract validates symlink targets lexically. (The defense against CVE-2025-29787 was broken in v7.2.0)

descriptions.value: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 7.2.0 until 9.0.0, ZipArchive::extract and ZipArchive::extract_unwrapped_root_dir use safe_prepare_path in src/read/zipfile.rs and simplified_components in src/path.rs to validate symbolic link targets with a lexical prefix comparison rather than resolving each intermediate link. An attacker who knows or can guess the absolute extraction destination can create a chain whose apparent target remains under the destination while an intermediate symlink resolves outside it, allowing attacker-controlled files to be created or overwritten with the extracting process's privileges. On Windows, discarded drive and UNC prefixes can permit a single-link escape when the process has SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege, such as through administrator rights or Developer Mode. This regression is distinct from CVE-2025-29787. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.32.0, ImageMediaIO passes attacker-controlled image bytes to Pillow through Image.open(BytesIO(data)) without restricting decoder selection, and the MIME label does not constrain the selected format. Image-capable request paths through parse_image() and fetch_image() can therefore dispatch an EPS payload to host components. cna.title: Twisted: Unauthenticated Remote Denial of Service in the Twisted IRC Server via an Unbounded Line Buffer

descriptions.value: Twisted is an event-based framework for internet applications, supporting Python 3.6+. Prior to 26.10.0rc1, twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC.dataReceived retains all bytes received without a line feed in its per-connection buffer and applies no maximum line length. The twisted.words.service.IRCUser server subclass inherits this behavior, and buffering occurs before PASS, NICK, or USER authentication commands. An unauthenticated connection can continuously grow the buffer until the shared server process runs out of memory and drops all users. This issue is fixed in version 26.10.0rc1.

cna.title: Control panel only API response emulation replaces "securityKey" and reaches server RCE

descriptions.value:
The app/process-api-response-headers action accepts fake Craft API response headers from any authenticated control panel user.



A non-admin user with only accessCp can place newline characters in X-Craft-Plugin-Licenses. Craft passes this value to its .env writer without removing the newlines.



This lets the user insert a new attacker-known CRAFT_SECURITY_KEY into .env. After Craft loads that key, the user can forge a signed login redirect containing a Twig system() callback.



This is different from the previous report. That report reads the existing key through a Twig sandbox bypass. This report replaces the key through fake API headers and CRLF injection. Fixing either source does not fix the other.

cna.title: epiphany: TLS certificate warning bypass via race in tlsErrorPage message handler

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Fernando Munoz for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Until a fixed Epiphany build is installed, avoid following links from untrusted sites to HTTPS destinations, and do not rely on Epiphany for sensitive sites when browsing untrusted content. Restrict network access for untrusted browsing where practical (https://cmetaxonomy.org/entries/CME-203.html). Restarting the browser clears any attacker-installed certificate exceptions for the session.

descriptions.value:
A race condition in Epiphany allows a malicious website to bypass the TLS/SSL certificate warning page.

Epiphany registers the main-world script message handler "tlsErrorPage" so its internal TLS error page can implement "Accept Risk and Proceed". The handler was registered immediately before loading the error page, leaving a brief window where the previously loaded untrusted origin could still call window.webkit.messageHandlers.tlsErrorPage.postMessage(...). The only authorization check compares a numeric WebKit page id that increments predictably; an attacker can burst-guess ids and approve a certificate exception with no user click.

If a victim visits malicious site A that redirects to site B with an invalid certificate, site A can, for a few milliseconds, disable TLS certificate error warnings for host B until Epiphany is restarted, enabling man-in-the-middle or site spoofing for that host.

Upstream report: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/work_items/2978
Proof of concept: https://beford.net/poc/ssl_poc.html
Fix: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/merge_requests/2245 (register handlers on LOAD_COMMITTED). No fixed release tagged yet; reporter and maintainer describe all current versions as affected. Maintainer notes the risky registration timing dates to commit 1da1caed (Epiphany 45.x era); before that the handlers were always registered and similarly reachable from web content.

cna.title: NULL pointer dereference in the BSD raw IPv6 send path when the destination table is full

descriptions.value: In Eclipse ThreadX NetX Duo versions 6.0 through 6.5.2.202603a, built with BSD raw socket and IPv6 support, the IPv6 raw send path uses the destination-table entry it adds without checking that the add succeeded. When the destination table is full and an off-link destination is reached through a default router whose neighbour cache entry is unknown, sending on an IPv6 raw socket with header inclusion dereferences a NULL pointer; a remote sender can fill the table, for example with ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages, and crash the sending thread.

cna.title: Session serializer mismatch can lead to remote code execution

descriptions.value: CAPEC-586 Object Injection

Session serializer mismatch can lead to remote code execution.

Session upload progress, when enabled, can store attacker-controlled data in a session key using the php_binary or php_serialize session serializer. If the same session is later read with the php serializer, because session.serialize_handler is changed at runtime or differs between applications sharing a session store, bytes inside the key can be passed to the unserializer. A remote attacker able to submit a multipart upload can inject objects, which may lead to code execution when the reading application contains a suitable gadget chain, or to session corruption or denial of service.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

cna.title: SumatraPDF: TLS hostname validation disabled in `HttpGet()`

descriptions.value: SumatraPDF is a multi-format reader for Windows. In version 3.6.1 and earlier, HttpGet() in src/base/Http_win.cpp unconditionally passes INTERNET_FLAG_IGNORE_CERT_CN_INVALID to WinINet, disabling hostname matching for HTTPS update metadata and crash-symbol requests while retaining certificate-chain validation. A network-positioned attacker with a Windows-trusted certificate for an attacker-controlled domain can impersonate the project's update host, inject promo text and a clickable URL before update metadata validation, and provide an attacker-controlled archive to ExtractSymbols(). Installer replacement is not directly possible because HttpGetToFile() validates TLS and MaybeStartUpdateDownload() restricts the download host. No fixed version is available as of this review.

references.name: Unbounded integer parsing in JSON.decode/1 enables CPU and memory exhaustion denial of service in Elixir

workarounds.value:
Decode untrusted JSON with an integer decoder that rejects long digit runs before conversion:

defmodule SafeJSON do
  def decode!(binary) do
    case JSON.decode(binary, :ok, integer: &safe_integer/1) do
      {decoded, :ok, ""} -> decoded
      _ -> raise ArgumentError, "invalid JSON"
    end
  end

  defp safe_integer(digits) when byte_size(digits) <= 1024, do: String.to_integer(digits)
  defp safe_integer(_digits), do: raise(ArgumentError, "integer too long")
end

In Phoenix, pass SafeJSON to Plug.Parsers as json_decoder instead of Phoenix.json_library().

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's JSON module allows an unauthenticated attacker who supplies a JSON document to cause a denial of service through CPU and memory exhaustion.

JSON.decode/1 and JSON.decode!/1 convert each integer literal with erlang:binary_to_integer/1 and do not bound its length. A literal of one million digits decodes successfully but costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string of the same length, so one request body of a few megabytes holds a scheduler for about a second. A literal of more than about 1.29 million digits raises SystemLimitError. Applications generated by phx.new decode request bodies with JSON in Plug.Parsers, before routing and authentication.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Default integer decoder

JSON.decode/1 and JSON.decode!/1 call JSON.decode/3 without an integer decoder. Up to the removal of Erlang/OTP 26 support, JSON.decode/3 used the vendored elixir_json module, whose default is fun erlang:binary_to_integer/1. It now calls OTP's :json.decode/3, which has the same default. The JSON.decode/3 documentation names &String.to_integer/1 as the default, which converts the same way.

2. Unbounded conversion

The decoder scans the digits of an integer literal and passes the whole run to the conversion. Nothing limits the run's length, so the cost grows faster than linearly with the number of digits. At one million digits an integer literal costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string literal of the same length. Above about 1.29 million digits the conversion raises SystemLimitError, which JSON.decode/3 does not catch.

3. Reach

phx.new sets config :phoenix, :json_library, JSON, and the generated endpoint passes Phoenix.json_library() to Plug.Parsers as json_decoder. Plug.Parsers runs before routing and authentication and accepts bodies up to 8 MB by default. It rescues the SystemLimitError into a 400 response after the CPU cost is spent. Jason, the previous default, rejects integer literals longer than its decoding_integer_digit_limit (1024 by default) before conversion.

cna.title: Zimbra Collaboration Suite Shared-File Mailbox Quota Accounting Error Enables Quota Exhaustion

credits.value: Jonah Burgess (CryptoCat), Senior Security Researcher, Rapid7

descriptions.value: A mailbox quota-accounting vulnerability in Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) allows an authenticated user to consume another user’s mailbox quota by repeatedly sharing and revoking a document. Creation of the recipient’s shared-file record charges the document size to mailbox-wide usage. Revocation deletes the record and reverses its folder counters without reversing the mailbox-wide charge. Repeated normal share notifications therefore accumulate quota usage after the visible records are gone. On accounts with a finite quota, this can prevent incoming mail and other size-increasing operations without recipient interaction. The issue affects ZCS 10.1.16 and 10.1.20.

cna.title: OpenNMS missing authorization on /api/v2 PATCH endpoints allows unauthenticated configuration changes

solutions.value: Upgrade to Horizon 36.0.4 or newer.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to Horizon 36.0.4 or newer.

descriptions.value:
A missing authorization vulnerability in OpenNMS Horizon allows configuration changes without authentication. The Spring Security policy for the /api/v2 REST API defines authorization rules for every HTTP method except PATCH, so the shipped @PATCH configuration endpoints for event configuration and SNMP data collection (which enable and disable event definitions and data-collection sources) are reachable with no authorization enforced. An unauthenticated attacker able to reach the web UI can disable event definitions and SNMP data collection, suppressing event and alarm generation and stopping metric collection - silently degrading monitoring and detection - with the change persisted and reloaded into the running system.



The solution is to upgrade to Horizon 36.0.4 or newer. Meridian and Horizon installation instructions state that they are intended for installation within an organization's private networks and should not be directly accessible from the Internet.

workarounds.value: Until upgrading, lower StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength well below its default of 20,000,000 characters so that oversized string tokens are rejected before number coercion, and apply wall-clock timeouts to parse and coercion operations. Because matching cost is quadratic in token length, a tight length bound substantially reduces worst-case cost. These are mitigations, not a complete fix.

descriptions.value:
NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre-validates "stringified numbers" with two regular expressions: PATTERN_FLOAT ([+-]?[0-9]*[\.]?[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?), present since 2.17.0, and PATTERN_FLOAT_TRAILING_DOT, added in 2.17.2. PATTERN_FLOAT places adjacent quantifiers over the same character class -- an optional [0-9]* run, an optional dot, then a required [0-9]+ run -- so input that ultimately fails to match forces Java's backtracking engine to retry every possible split point of the digit run. 



Matching cost therefore grows with the square of the input length. 



An attacker who can supply JSON that an application deserializes into a numeric target type reaches this method through jackson-databind's default String-to-number coercion (StdDeserializer and NumberDeserializers for BigDecimal, BigInteger, Double and Float). 



Because StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength defaults to 20,000,000 characters, no constraint bounds the input before it reaches the regex. 



Testing by the reporter confirmed O(n^2) growth across five consecutive input-size doublings, with a single 160,000-character string consuming roughly 74 seconds in one call; a small number of concurrent requests of ordinary body size can therefore exhaust a server's request-handling thread pool. 



The affected method does not exist before 2.17.0, so 2.16.x and earlier releases are not affected. 



The fix replaces both regular expressions with a hand-rolled single-pass scan.

cna.title: sctp: drop a chunk if its transport was removed

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A remote SCTP peer reaches the bug via received packets in sctp_rcv() on internet-facing SCTP servers and telecom endpoints; DATA that already resolved a transport is processed after an authenticated ASCONF DEL-IP (or COOKIE-ECHO restart) has removed that peer.
AC:L - The attacker controls both sides of the race by sending ASCONF DEL-IP (or a restart that calls sctp_assoc_rm_peer) and a DATA chunk whose lookup already holds the doomed transport; the backlog path is FIFO-deterministic while the socket is in a syscall, and the direct path is a bh_lock_sock race the attacker creates.
PR:N - Exploitation requires only a network-reachable established SCTP association; no local Linux credentials, capabilities, or namespaces are needed, and SCTP-AUTH keys used for ASCONF come from the handshake the peer itself performs.
UI:N - Inbound SCTP packets are processed automatically in softirq or socket backlog on a listening or already-associated endpoint; no victim user action such as opening a file or mounting a device is required.
S:U - Impact is kernel memory corruption and potential privilege escalation within the host SCTP stack; it does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:H - DATA processing plants the removed transport into asoc->peer.last_data_from; after the lookup reference is dropped the object is RCU-freed, and the next delayed SACK dereferences the freed sctp_transport in sctp_outq_select_transport(), a UAF that enables arbitrary kernel disclosure via heap grooming.
I:H - sctp_outq_select_transport() does list_add_tail() into the freed send_ready field, and sctp_packet_config()/sctp_transport_burst_limited() write vtag, pathmtu, cwnd, and burst_limited into the reclaimed slab object, yielding arbitrary write and control-flow hijack primitives.
A:H - Dereferencing the freed transport during delayed SACK transmission can immediately oops or panic the kernel, and the UAF can be triggered repeatedly by a malicious SCTP peer.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: drop a chunk if its transport was removed

sctp_rcv() resolves the transport once per packet and leaves it in
chunk->transport. The lookup reference, or the one sctp_add_backlog() takes
if the socket is owned by userspace, keeps it around until the chunk has
been processed.

An authenticated ASCONF DEL-IP can remove it in the meantime.
sctp_assoc_rm_peer() takes the transport out of the association and calls
sctp_transport_free(), which tags it dead and drops the reference the
association held. There is a window on both paths: the packet can sit on
the socket backlog, and on the direct path the lookup completes before
bh_lock_sock().

The DATA chunk in that packet puts the removed transport back into
asoc->peer.last_data_from. Once the packet is done that reference goes
away and the transport is freed by RCU, so the next delayed SACK carries
the pointer into the SACK chunk and sctp_outq_select_transport() reads the
freed transport's state.

Drop the chunk in sctp_inq_push(), next to the existing rcvr->dead check.
Both paths reach it with the association's socket lock held. The peer
retransmits it.

cna.title: smb: client: clear ce->tgthint in free_tgts()

scenarios.value:
AV:N - The dangling ce->tgthint is created while handling FSCTL_DFS_GET_REFERRALS/TRANS2_GET_DFS_REFERRAL replies from a remote SMB server over TCP/445 (smb2_get_dfs_refer → cache_refresh_path → update_cache_entry_locked → free_tgts). A malicious, compromised, or MITM'd DFS server reaches this purely over the network.
AC:L - A hostile DFS server controls referral TTL (down to CACHE_MIN_TTL), target lists, and TCP resets that drive dfs_cache_refresh and reconnect into update_cache_entry_locked; after free_tgts() the later get_tgt_name()/dfs_cache_noreq_update_tgthint() use is deterministic, and the attacker can size and retry referrals to leave the stale hint and reclaim the slab.
PR:N - The attacker is the remote SMB/DFS peer (or a MITM on an unsigned session) and needs no account, capability, or local privileges on the victim; the client authenticates to that server, and the kernel DFS cache parses the reply regardless of which local user owns the mount.
UI:N - Once a DFS CIFS mount exists (fstab, autofs/systemd automount, enterprise DFS, cifsroot), dfs_cache_refresh delayed work and reconnect-driven cifs_tree_connect()/dfs_cache_noreq_find() use the stale tgthint automatically after a server-induced refresh or TCP drop, with no further user action.
S:U - The use-after-free is of kmalloc'd cache_dfs_tgt objects in the client kernel heap and remains in the same host kernel security authority; it does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundary.
C:H - get_tgt_name() and dfs_cache_noreq_update_tgthint() dereference the freed cache_dfs_tgt (t->name). Reclaiming that slab with attacker-controlled SMB allocations yields an arbitrary kernel read via kstrdup/strcasecmp of a sprayed name pointer.
I:H - Use-after-free of the heap cache_dfs_tgt enables heap spraying and overlapping live objects; the dangling hint is also copied into DFS referral state and used for failover tree-connect, giving a write/control-flow primitive once the object is reclaimed.
A:H - Dereferencing the freed cache_dfs_tgt from reconnect (cifs_tree_connect → dfs_cache_noreq_find) or dfs_cache_find oopses or panics the client kernel, and a malicious server can retrigger it on every refresh or reconnect.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: clear ce->tgthint in free_tgts()

When free_tgts() frees all structures in ce->tlist, ce->tgthint
is left pointing to one of the freed cache_dfs_tgt structures.

If ce->tgthint is not reset before it is used later, it results
in a use-after-free.

Set ce->tgthint to NULL in free_tgts() after the elements are
freed to reflect that no elements remain.

cna.title: SUNRPC: harden gss_unwrap_resp_priv length checks

scenarios.value:
AV:N - gss_unwrap_resp_priv() runs in the Linux NFS/SUNRPC client while decoding RPCSEC_GSS privacy (krb5p) replies; a malicious or compromised NFS server supplies the crafted opaque_len and wrap token over the existing TCP/UDP/RDMA RPC connection.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the reply, including opaque_len and the cleartext RFC 4121 header, and a single response can make offset+opaque_len wrap in u32 or fall below GSS_KRB5_TOK_HDR_LEN; no race or layout beyond the attacker’s control is required.
PR:N - The attacker is the remote RPC/NFS peer that already holds the GSS session keys needed to pass gss_validate(); no local account, user namespace, or capability on the victim client is required.
UI:N - Once a krb5p NFS mount or other SUNRPC GSS-privacy client is already in use, normal client RPCs elicit replies the attacker can craft; no extra victim action is needed at attack time.
S:U - Out-of-bounds reads, rotate/decrypt memory corruption, and crashes stay inside the victim kernel’s SUNRPC client and do not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:H - A short or wrapped opaque_len makes gss_krb5_unwrap_v2() read past the token at ptr+4/ptr+6 and feeds rotate_left()/decrypt with wrapped lengths, disclosing adjacent kernel memory; unwrap cleanup can also memmove nearly UINT_MAX bytes.
I:H - The same wrapped lengths drive rotate_left() writes, CBC/AEAD decrypt over an unbounded xdr subsegment (xdr_buf_subsegment’s error is ignored), and gss_krb5_unwrap_v2()’s unsigned movelen underflow into a near-4GiB memmove, enabling kernel memory corruption.
A:H - rotate_left() can divide-by-zero on a zero-length subbuffer, spin in a multi-gigabyte kernel loop on a wrapped subsegment, or oops/panic on the huge memmove or out-of-bounds header access.

cna.title: nvme-tcp: do not accept C2HData based on blk_rq_payload_bytes() alone

scenarios.value:
AV:N - The nvme-tcp host receive path parses C2HData PDUs from a remote NVMe/TCP target over a routable TCP connection (typically port 4420); a malicious or compromised target, or an on-path attacker injecting into the stream, triggers the bug from the network.
AC:L - A malicious target can advertise WRITE_ZEROES, wait for tag reuse after a data command, and send C2HData for that in-flight WRITE_ZEROES; leftover iterator state is deterministic because driver-private fields are not cleared on reuse, so no race or memory-layout luck is required.
PR:N - NVMe/TCP authentication (TLS, DH-HMAC-CHAP) is optional and off by default; the vulnerable copy runs on C2HData from the connected peer, which needs no credentials or privileges on the victim host.
UI:N - Once the host is connected to the target as persistent storage, ordinary filesystem and block I/O generate WRITE_ZEROES commands; the attacker sends the crafted PDU without any further victim action.
S:U - The stale-iterator write corrupts memory in the same host kernel security authority; this is not a VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundary crossing.
C:H - nvme_tcp_recv_data() writes attacker-controlled C2HData through a leftover iov_iter into pages from a previously completed command on the same tag, a use-after-free of those buffers that can be turned into an arbitrary read via heap reuse.
I:H - The copy is a use-after-free / wild write of attacker-chosen contents and length into reused kernel or page-cache memory, which is exploitable for arbitrary write and control-flow hijacking.
A:H - The same stale-iterator write was reproduced as a KASAN wild-memory-access in _copy_to_iter from nvme_tcp_io_work and can oops or panic the host kernel.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-tcp: do not accept C2HData based on blk_rq_payload_bytes() alone

Commit 25e5cb780e62 ("nvme-tcp: fix possible crash in write_zeroes
processing") established that blk_rq_payload_bytes() must not be read
without first checking blk_rq_nr_phys_segments(), and recorded the
result in nvme_tcp_setup_cmd_pdu() as req->data_len. The receive side
was left as it was.

The two differ for REQ_OP_WRITE_ZEROES, which has no physical segments
but a non-zero blk_rq_bytes(), so setup leaves req->iter untouched
while the receive gate lets a C2HData through and nvme_tcp_recv_data()
copies into whatever the previous command on that tag left there. The
driver-private area is zeroed only when the tag set is allocated.

Reproduced with a test target that leaves a residual iterator on a tag
and then sends a C2HData for a WRITE_ZEROES command on the same tag:

old test is what rejects a C2HData naming a tag that is no longer in
flight, because blk_update_request() zeroes rq->__data_len on

survive completion, so they cannot stand in for it. Setup initialises
the iterator only when both req->curr_bio and req->data_len are set, so
the gate now tests the same two.

cna.title: sctp: stop processing a packet once its association is deleted

scenarios.value:
AV:N - The UAF is reached from sctp_rcv() when a remote peer sends a bundled SCTP packet (COOKIE-ECHO, SHUTDOWN, SHUTDOWN-ACK, then another chunk) to a listening internet-facing SCTP endpoint; no local syscall or link-local medium is required.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the four-way handshake and the bundled chunk order that creates, caches, then deletes the association in one packet; forcing that packet onto the socket backlog is done with concurrent associations or recv/accept load the attacker generates, with no victim-only race.
PR:N - COOKIE-ECHO is the unauthenticated SCTP handshake completion using only the INIT-ACK cookie as anti-spoofing; a network peer needs no Linux account, capability, or namespace privilege on the victim host.
UI:N - The kernel automatically processes inbound SCTP chunks in sctp_endpoint_bh_rcv()/sctp_do_sm(); no victim mount, file open, or other interactive action is required.
S:U - Impact is kernel heap use-after-free of sctp_association/sctp_transport on the host; it does not cross a VM, container, or IOMMU boundary.
C:H - After DELETE_TCB the next bundled chunk reads freed asoc->state and other association fields and is passed into sctp_do_sm(); UAF of these slab objects enables heap grooming for arbitrary kernel disclosure.
I:H - The same loop writes last_time_heard on the RCU-freed transport and mutates freed asoc fields (stats, last_data_from) before sctp_do_sm() runs with the dangling pointer, yielding a standard UAF write/control-flow primitive.
A:H - Dereferencing the freed association and transport in the endpoint receive loop can oops or panic the kernel, and a remote peer can repeat the bundled packet against any listening SCTP service.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: stop processing a packet once its association is deleted

sctp_endpoint_bh_rcv() looks the association up only when chunk->asoc is
NULL, and caches the result in chunk->asoc and chunk->transport without
taking a reference.

A packet that matches no association is handed to the endpoint, so a peer
can bundle COOKIE ECHO, SHUTDOWN and SHUTDOWN ACK in one packet. The
COOKIE ECHO creates the association, the SHUTDOWN chunk caches it, and
with the outqueue empty the SHUTDOWN ACK reaches sctp_sf_do_9_2_final(),
so the association and its transports are freed.

The endpoint loop has no counterpart to the asoc->base.dead check in
sctp_assoc_bh_rcv(). The next chunk writes to last_time_heard in the freed
transport and is then passed to sctp_do_sm() with the freed association.
The transport is freed through RCU, so this needs the packet to come off
the socket backlog, where the loop runs in task context.

The endpoint loop cannot do the same check: it holds no reference on the
association, so reading asoc->base.dead would itself be a use-after-free.
Mark the packet for discard in the command interpreter, just before it
deletes the association. That is also before sctp_inq_free() releases the
chunk on the association receive path.

sctp_sf_do_5_2_4_dupcook() issues SCTP_CMD_DELETE_TCB for the temporary
association, while the one the packet belongs to stays alive. A restarting
peer can bundle DATA behind its COOKIE ECHO, so compare against
chunk->asoc and leave that case alone.

cna.title: nouveau/gem: reserve the bo in the info ioctl around the vma lookup

scenarios.value:
AV:L - Reached only via local DRM ioctls on a nouveau render node (/dev/dri/renderD*): DRM_IOCTL_NOUVEAU_GEM_INFO (nouveau_gem_ioctl_info→nouveau_gem_info) racing DRM_IOCTL_GEM_CLOSE (nouveau_gem_object_close). Not reachable from network protocols, adjacent radios, or physical buses.
AC:L - The attacker controls both sides of the race with threads that GEM_INFO and GEM_CLOSE the same handle, so close kfree()s the nouveau_vma while info still uses it. Skipping UVMM (legacy GEM_NEW) selects the vulnerable path; no victim timing or rare config is required.
PR:L - NOUVEAU_GEM_INFO and GEM_CLOSE are DRM_RENDER_ALLOW with no DRM_ROOT_ONLY or capability checks. Any unprivileged local user who can open the nouveau render node (typical render/video group or uaccess ACL) can trigger it without init-namespace root.
UI:N - Exploitation needs only the attacker opening their own DRM client, creating a GEM BO, and racing GEM_INFO against GEM_CLOSE on that handle; no separate victim action is required.
S:U - The use-after-free corrupts kernel heap state (struct nouveau_vma) inside the host nouveau driver. Impact stays in the same kernel authority; this is not a VM escape or IOMMU/DMA isolation bypass.
C:H - Use-after-free of struct nouveau_vma lets GEM_INFO read vma->addr after kfree, and concurrent walks of nvbo->vma_list can follow attacker-reused slab objects, enabling kernel memory disclosure as with other UAFs.
I:H - UAF of the VMA plus concurrent list_del/list_del_init on nvbo->vma_list enables heap spraying and list-pointer corruption, supporting arbitrary kernel writes and control-flow hijack as with other kernel UAFs.
A:H - Dereferencing a freed nouveau_vma in GEM_INFO or walking a concurrently deleted vma_list causes a kernel oops/panic; the attacker can repeat the race to crash or hang the system.

In the non-uvmm path, there could be a race between the info lookup

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Hugo before v0.165.0 Symlink Confinement Bypass via resources.Get

descriptions.value: Hugo is a static site generator. In versions after v0.123.0 and before v0.165.0, symlinks in parent directories were not dropped during direct resource lookups, allowing path confinement to be bypassed. An attacker who can place — or who convinces a site author to place — a symlink inside a mounted directory (for example, in a locally vendored theme under themes/) can cause functions that perform direct lookups, such as resources.Get and os.ReadFile, to follow that symlink and read files outside the intended project boundaries, disclosing their contents in the built site. Themes mounted as Go modules fetched from GitHub have symlinks stripped on download and are not affected, and multi-directory walks (e.g. content/asset walking) are not affected. This issue is an incomplete-fix follow-up to GHSA-c3wq-j5vh-68rc and GHSA-fw87-fv5r-9fpw; it is fixed in v0.165.0.

cna.title: sunrpc: route to a populated pool in svc_pool_for_cpu()

scenarios.value:
AV:N - nfsd is the in-kernel NFS server; inbound TCP/UDP/RDMA traffic hits svc_tcp_listen_data_ready/svc_data_ready then svc_xprt_enqueue() and svc_pool_for_cpu() before any RPC decode, so a remote peer reaches the bug over the wire.
AC:L - On NUMA nfsd hosts using pernode/percpu pools with fewer threads than pools, a remote peer can open connections or send datagrams until RSS/softirq lands the listener or shared UDP xprt on an empty pool; the attacker controls that fan-out and no race or layout luck is required.
PR:N - Enqueue runs in the socket data_ready path on the first TCP connect or UDP datagram to nfsd, before RPC parsing or AUTH_SYS/RPCSEC_GSS, so an unauthenticated network peer needs no local account or capability.
UI:N - No victim action is required; an already-running NFS server automatically processes inbound connections and packets through the sunrpc transport callbacks.
S:U - The hang is confined to the host kernel's sunrpc/nfsd threads and sockets and does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:N - This is a transport-scheduling hang with no memory corruption, out-of-bounds access, or other primitive that could disclose kernel or file data.
I:N - A transport stuck on a threadless pool is never serviced, so RPC operations are not executed and no kernel or filesystem state is modified.
A:H - A transport enqueued on a threadless pool stays XPT_BUSY and is never dequeued; aging skips busy sockets, so a stuck listener or shared UDP xprt permanently stops NFS accept/recv until nfsd restarts.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sunrpc: route to a populated pool in svc_pool_for_cpu()

svc_set_num_threads() spreads the requested threads evenly across the
service's pools (base = nrservs / sv_nrpools).  When a service runs
fewer threads than it has pools -- e.g. an nfsd configured with fewer
threads than the host has NUMA nodes while running in "pernode" or
"percpu" mode -- the trailing pools are left with no threads at all.

svc_xprt_enqueue() selects a pool from the CPU servicing the transport,
queues the transport on that pool's sp_xprts, and only wakes a thread
from the same pool.  Each thread services exclusively its own pool, so a
transport that lands on a threadless pool is enqueued on sp_xprts and
never picked up: the connection hangs indefinitely.

Have svc_pool_for_cpu() skip pools that currently have no threads,
falling back to the next populated pool.  This trades NUMA locality for
a guarantee that the work is actually serviced.  sp_nrthreads is only
updated under the service mutex; the lockless read here is a best-effort
routing hint, so annotate it with data_race().

descriptions.value: UTF8DataInputJsonParser._reportInvalidToken() in FasterXML jackson-core builds the offending-token text for its error message by appending Java identifier characters to a StringBuilder in a loop that has no upper bound. Unlike the three sibling parser implementations, including UTF8StreamJsonParser, it never consults ErrorReportConfiguration.getMaxErrorTokenLength() (default 256). A malformed token supplied to a parser created through JsonFactory.createParser(DataInput) is therefore accumulated in full. No StreamReadConstraints setting mitigates this: maxDocumentLength cannot be applied to DataInput sources at all, and maxStringLength does not cover this path because the accumulation bypasses ReadConstrainedTextBuffer. The reporter measured a 20,000,109-character exception message from a 20-million-character malformed token on the DataInput path, against 367 characters for identical input on the InputStream path. Scaling the payload drives the StringBuilder, which also incurs byte-to-char expansion and internal array doubling, to many times the raw payload size and can trigger OutOfMemoryError for the whole JVM. cna.title: nfsd: fix clock domain mismatch in clients_still_reclaiming()

scenarios.value:
AV:N - nfsd processes NFSv4 COMPOUND OPEN over TCP (typically port 2049). A remote peer reaches clients_still_reclaiming() by sending CLAIM_PREVIOUS OPEN or reclaim LOCK, which sets NFSD_NET_SOMEBODY_RECLAIMED and prevents grace from ending.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the reclaim OPEN/LOCK RPCs that keep NFSD_NET_SOMEBODY_RECLAIMED set; no race or memory layout is required. Grace always starts with nfsd, and the broken REALTIME-vs-BOOTTIME deadline never fires, so the attacker can extend it at will.
PR:N - Default nfsd exports accept AUTH_SYS/AUTH_NULL with no credentials. An unauthenticated network peer that is or becomes a recorded NFSv4 client can send CLAIM_PREVIOUS OPEN; no server account or capability is required.
UI:N - Exploitation takes only attacker-sent NFSv4 RPCs after nfsd starts; no victim user action such as mounting or opening a file is required.
S:U - The impact stays in the same kernel nfsd/lockd grace state. This is a service denial on the NFS server, not a VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundary crossing.
C:N - The bug only miscompares grace deadlines and extends the grace period. It does not disclose kernel memory or file contents.
I:N - No unauthorized modification of kernel or file data occurs. Other clients are blocked from new mutating operations, which is an availability effect rather than an integrity violation.
A:H - Successful reclaim OPENs hold nfsd in grace indefinitely because the double-lease deadline never expires, so non-reclaim OPEN/REMOVE/RENAME/SETXATTR and lockd grace return NFS4ERR_GRACE and fully deny NFSv4 service to other clients.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: fix clock domain mismatch in clients_still_reclaiming()

clients_still_reclaiming() computes a deadline from nn->boot_time
(CLOCK_REALTIME, ~1.7 billion) but compares it against
ktime_get_boottime_seconds() (CLOCK_BOOTTIME, seconds since boot).
The comparison is always false — it would take ~54 years of uptime
for BOOTTIME to exceed the REALTIME-derived deadline.

This means any client can hold the server in grace indefinitely by
sending CLAIM_PREVIOUS OPEN requests, blocking all non-reclaim
operations for all other clients.

Add boot_time_bt (CLOCK_BOOTTIME) alongside the existing boot_time
and use it for the deadline computation. boot_time (CLOCK_REALTIME)
is preserved for its cl_boot clientid-nonce role.

cna.title: dm array: validate array block headers on read

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The bug is reached when the kernel reads attacker-crafted dm-array metadata from a local block device during device-mapper activation (dm-cache dm_cache_load_mappings, dm-clone bitset load, or dm-era array resize), not via a network protocol.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the on-disk array-block header (nr_entries, max_entries, value_size) and can compute a matching checksum, so activation deterministically walks off the dm-bufio buffer; there is no race or attacker-uncontrollable memory layout.
PR:L - Device-mapper ioctls require init-namespace CAP_SYS_ADMIN and are not reachable via user namespaces, but the malformed data is on-disk metadata, so the attacker only needs write access to the backing store (loop file, VM/container disk, iSCSI/NBD LUN) that a dm-cache/dm-era/dm-clone stack is built on.
UI:N - Once corrupt metadata is on the backing store, LVM/udev autoactivation, boot, or reattachment of the volume loads mappings without a separate victim action such as mounting a filesystem or opening a file.
S:U - The out-of-bounds access is confined to kernel dm-bufio metadata buffers on the same host; this is ordinary kernel memory corruption, not a VM escape, IOMMU bypass, or sandbox boundary crossing.
C:H - dm_array_cursor_next() takes its loop bound from on-disk nr_entries while element_at() is unguarded pointer arithmetic, so a too-large count keeps the cursor in one block and reads past the dm-bufio data buffer (typically a 4K slab/page) for every cache block at activation, an unbounded kernel out-of-bounds read.
I:H - Unchecked headers let fill_ablock()/trim_ablock() hit BUG_ON on resize, and out-of-bounds mapping, hint, and bitset values from adjacent kernel memory are installed into the cache policy and then used for origin/cache I/O, giving a memory-corruption integrity primitive.
A:H - Walking off the dm-bufio buffer causes a kernel oops or KASAN panic, and an undersized on-disk max_entries hits BUG_ON in fill_ablock() and trim_ablock() during array resize at activation.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

dm array: validate array block headers on read

array_block_check() validates blocknr and csum and nothing else, while
node_check(), next to it, has bounded the structural fields since both
were written. dm_array_cursor_next() takes its loop bound from the
on-disk nr_entries and element_at() is unguarded pointer arithmetic, so
a count larger than the block holds keeps the cursor in one block while
the index grows past it and the read walks off the dm-bufio buffer --
dm_cache_load_mappings() drives it once per cache block at activation.

Check the header against itself: reject a zero value_size, require
max_entries to equal calc_max_entries() for that value_size and block
size, and require nr_entries to fit. Equality rather than an upper bound,
since a count below the real capacity trips BUG_ON() in fill_ablock() and
trim_ablock(). Metadata dm-array writes satisfies all three.

descriptions.description: CWE-409 Improper handling of highly compressed data (data amplification)

descriptions.value:
Publishing limits the compressed size of a VSIX (ovsx.publishing.max-content-size, 512 MB by default) but nothing limited how large an entry becomes when opened.




On the first request to /vscode/unpkg/{namespace}/{extension}/{version}/{path}, WebResourceService opened the entry with ZipFile.getInputStream() and passed the decompressed stream to Files.copy(), which ran to the end of the stream without counting bytes written. The result was cached under java.io.tmpdir, and that cache evicted by entry count (150), not by size, so it placed no bound on disk usage.




A publisher with access only to their own namespace could therefore upload a small, highly compressible VSIX and cause the server to write far larger files to the temp filesystem — repeating with different files or versions, since a repeat request is served from the cache.




Impact observed: the temp filesystem filled; requests for files not already cached returned 500 with No space left on device; a failed extraction left a partial cache file that blocked later attempts at that path; publishing failed with Failed to read extension file. Metadata and already-cached files kept working, and the server did not stop.




Triggering the extraction needs no authentication — only the upload does.
